chunks: "Transmission line theory is circuit theory for wires that are electrically long.
Normally I treat a wire as a node: the voltage is the same everywhere along it at the same instant. That assumption is really saying the signal arrives instantly.
But a signal on a PCB trace travels at roughly half the speed of light, so a 15 cm trace takes about a nanosecond.
If my edge rate is also around a nanosecond, the far end hasn't even heard about the edge when the near end is already half way through it.
So instead I model the trace as a chain of tiny series inductors and shunt capacitors, a distributed model. That gives me a wave equation instead of a lumped equation.

Out of it comes two numbers that describe the line, the characteristic impedance Z 0 equals square root of L' over C' and the delay, and one rule: wherever the impedance changes, part of the wave reflects, with coefficient equals (Z L minus Z 0) over (Z L plus Z 0) .
We need it because reflections turn into ringing, overshoot and false edges. With TL theory I can pick trace geometry for a controlled impedance, add termination, and avoid stubs.
When the trace is short compared with the edge, it collapses back to lumped analysis, so it's the more general theory rather than a competing one."
